question: For AdamW language-model pretraining with a known token budget, when and why does warmup followed by linear learning-rate decay to zero outperform cosine or linear decay to a nonzero floor and continuous schedules such as WSD?

key_findings.claim: At compute-optimal and overtraining token budgets, tuned linear decay-to-zero is consistently better than tuned 10x decay, while very short low-TPP runs can favor retaining a nonzero learning rate.
key_findings.evidence: For 610M-parameter models at 20 tokens per parameter, the best Linear-D2Z validation loss is 0.77% lower than best Linear-10x. At 111M and 2 TPP, D2Z is worse, but its advantage grows with duration; at 200 TPP it exceeds the best 10x result by 1.6%. Across 111M, 610M, and 1.7B models, the gap increases with TPP.

key_findings.claim: Linear is only modestly but consistently better than cosine when both decay to zero; linear is not universally better when the schedules stop at one tenth of peak.
key_findings.evidence: Across the six peak-rate settings in Table 1, Linear-D2Z slightly beats Cosine-D2Z each time, whereas Cosine-10x slightly beats Linear-10x. This isolates an interaction between decay shape and endpoint rather than a blanket advantage for linear schedules.

key_findings.claim: The empirical gains can be large enough to dominate additional training tokens in the studied regime, but extrapolations to frontier models are projections rather than direct measurements.
key_findings.evidence: A 610M D2Z model trained for 80 TPP beats a 10x model trained for 200 TPP on training and validation loss, implying 60% fewer pretraining FLOPs for that comparison. Its average downstream score, 43.54%, is also close to the 200-TPP 10x model's 43.46%. The largest main-model experiment is 1.7B, with appendix scaling fits up to 2.75B rather than a direct 7B or 70B test.

key_findings.claim: Under AdamW, the full learning-rate and weight-decay trajectory determines a weighted combination of past normalized updates, offering a useful explanation for schedule-dependent recency and noise averaging.
key_findings.evidence: Unrolling AdamW gives coefficient c_{t,i}=eta_i lambda times the product of later factors (1-eta_j lambda). Linear D2Z produces flatter late-stage coefficients than abrupt step or cosine changes, and frozen-weight evaluation on ordered training batches shows Constant and 10x models fitting the latest batches more strongly than D2Z.

anchors.section: 3.1 AdamW as convex combination of weight updates

key_findings.claim: D2Z reduces peak-learning-rate sensitivity across token budgets, weight decay, and batch size, and outperforms the tested WSD branch at 80 TPP, but it requires advance knowledge of the stopping budget.
key_findings.evidence: Loss bowls and optima move much less for D2Z than for Constant or 10x as TPP and batch size change. At 610M/80 TPP, optimal D2Z is about 0.84% lower loss than optimal WSD. The paper acknowledges that D2Z must be parameterized by the planned final step and may fail when high peak rates are unstable.

method.core_idea: Sweep both peak learning rate and schedule shape/end ratio over language-model sizes and token budgets, then interpret AdamW parameters as a time-varying exponential moving average of normalized weight updates.
method.mechanism: The study compares constant, inverse-square-root, step, cyclic, WSD, cosine, and linear schedules with nonzero or zero endpoints. By expanding decoupled weight decay recursively, it derives the contribution of each historical normalized update and connects longer averaging windows to late-training gradient-noise reduction.
assumptions: Validation cross-entropy and the selected downstream suite adequately rank pretraining schedules.
Per-schedule peak-rate sweeps are broad enough to identify comparable optima.
The AdamW update-mixture view captures the dominant reason schedule shape matters despite nonlinear, nonstationary neural-network training.
Small-to-mid-scale GPT-like results and fitted loss scaling trends transfer to much larger production models.
Tokens per parameter is a useful proxy for the transition from bias-dominated to gradient-noise-dominated training.

techniques.role: Avoids comparing learning-rate schedules at a peak rate tuned for a different endpoint.
Maps the full LR/weight-decay trajectory to explicit contributions from historical normalized updates.
Measures how schedule ranking changes from short runs to compute-optimal and overtrained regimes.
Evaluates frozen checkpoints on original ordered batches to test whether schedules overweight recent updates.
Fits loss-to-FLOPs power laws separately for D2Z and 10x decay.

evaluations.setting: GPT-like ALiBi/SwiGLU models from 111M to 1.7B parameters on SlimPajama, primarily with muP, across 2-200 tokens per parameter and peak-rate sweeps.
evaluations.result: D2Z loses at very low TPP but becomes best by compute-optimal 20 TPP; its advantage over 10x grows with duration and reaches 3.05% at 1.7B/80 TPP at the proxy-tuned rate.
evaluations.baseline: Optimally tuned constant, inverse-square-root, cosine/linear 10x, and cosine D2Z schedules.

evaluations.setting: 610M models at 80 and 200 TPP, including evaluation on MMLU, commonsense, reading, truthfulness, and bias tasks.
evaluations.metric: Training/validation loss and mean downstream percentage.
evaluations.result: D2Z at 80 TPP beats 10x at 200 TPP on loss and approximately matches its downstream average; D2Z at 200 TPP attains the best downstream average, 45.00%.
evaluations.baseline: Linear 10x at matched or 2.5x larger token budgets.

evaluations.setting: 610M/80-TPP comparisons against WSD and cyclic schedules, plus batch-size and weight-decay grids.
evaluations.metric: Optimal validation loss and movement/flatness of the optimal peak-rate basin.
evaluations.result: D2Z is about 0.84% better than optimal WSD and is less sensitive to batch size, weight decay, and training duration.
evaluations.baseline: WSD, cyclic, constant, and 10x schedules with their own peak-rate sweeps.

evaluations.setting: Four model sizes up to 2.75B at 20 TPP with Llama-style architecture, 8192-token context, and bilingual/code data.
evaluations.metric: Power-law slope of validation loss versus pretraining FLOPs.
evaluations.result: The fitted D2Z slope is roughly 2.5% steeper than 10x, supporting—but not directly validating—larger-scale extrapolation.
evaluations.baseline: Linear decay to one tenth of peak.

limitations: The largest direct comparisons are far below current frontier scale; claims about Llama-2-7B compute savings and 70B improvement are extrapolations.
Most schedule runs share one random seed, with multi-seed evidence relegated to a smaller appendix check.
D2Z needs a predetermined stopping step and is unsuitable for arbitrary checkpoint extraction without branching or redesign.
The main results use AdamW and may not transfer to approximate second-order or other non-decoupled optimizers.
The EMA derivation is exact algebra, but interpreting coefficient flatness as causal noise reduction is a conceptual model rather than a nonlinear optimization theorem.
Low-data and unstable-training regimes can favor less decay or prevent use of D2Z's higher optimal peak rate.
failure_modes: Reusing a peak rate tuned for 10x decay can make D2Z appear worse or destabilize training.
A short proxy run at low TPP can reverse the schedule ranking and lead to the wrong production choice.
Numerical instability at the higher D2Z optimum can erase the theoretical benefit; the NanoGPT replication required moving from bfloat16 to float32.
Training that must stop unpredictably can end before the zero-decay cooldown and yield a poor checkpoint.
Data ordering or distribution shift late in training can interact with D2Z's historical averaging in ways not captured by shuffled held-out loss.
reusable_insights: Schedule comparisons must jointly tune the peak rate and decay endpoint; otherwise the schedule is confounded with a mismatched optimizer scale.
Report schedule quality as a function of tokens per parameter rather than extrapolating from cheap short runs.
Unrolling optimizer state into historical-update coefficients is a low-cost diagnostic for candidate schedules before expensive training.
Learning-rate schedules can change hyperparameter-transfer laws, including apparent batch-size scaling of the optimal rate.
Compute-savings claims are strongest when a shorter-run schedule beats a longer-run baseline on both validation loss and downstream evaluations.
open_questions: Does linear D2Z retain its edge at 7B-70B scale with modern architectures, data mixtures, and multiple seeds?
Can a stopping-time-agnostic controller reproduce D2Z's update coefficients while yielding strong checkpoints at any time?
How should peak rate, weight decay, and batch size be jointly adapted as gradient noise changes during high-TPP training?
Does D2Z change memorization, calibration, data-order sensitivity, or rare-domain retention beyond average loss?
Can the update-mixture account generate falsifiable predictions for optimizers without decoupled weight decay?

competitive_landscape.title: Optimal Linear Decay Learning Rate Schedules and Further Refinements
competitive_landscape.relationship: Closest direct predecessor deriving linear decay as a worst-case-optimal schedule and benchmarking it across deep-learning problems including LMs.
competitive_landscape.difference: Defazio et al. provide broader schedule theory and task coverage; the target focuses on LLM token budgets, jointly sweeps endpoint and peak rate, and adds an AdamW historical-update explanation.

competitive_landscape.title: Understanding Warmup-Stable-Decay Learning Rates: A River Valley Loss Landscape Perspective
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct alternative for obtaining language-model checkpoints at multiple compute budgets through a stable branch and rapid decay branches.
competitive_landscape.difference: WSD-S optimizes flexibility across unknown/multiple stopping budgets and offers a loss-landscape theory; the target optimizes a single known budget and finds full-run linear D2Z lower-loss in its tested comparison.

competitive_landscape.title: The Road Less Scheduled
competitive_landscape.relationship: Schedule-free optimizer competitor designed to avoid dependence on the final training step while retaining scheduled-optimizer performance.
competitive_landscape.difference: Schedule-Free AdamW couples iterate averaging and optimization without a prescribed horizon and wins broad AlgoPerf tests; the target retains standard AdamW and argues a horizon-aware linear schedule is best for its LLM setting.

competitive_landscape.title: How to set AdamW's weight decay as you scale model and dataset size
competitive_landscape.relationship: Immediate theoretical foundation for viewing AdamW weights as an EMA of updates and scaling the associated timescale.
competitive_landscape.difference: Wang and Aitchison emphasize weight-decay scaling across dataset/model size and validate mostly vision plus NanoGPT; the target generalizes the coefficient calculation to time-varying LR schedules and conducts larger LLM schedule sweeps.

competitive_landscape.title: Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models
competitive_landscape.relationship: Defines the compute-optimal tokens-per-parameter regime and popularized the cosine-to-10%-of-peak recipe used as the target's main baseline.
competitive_landscape.difference: Chinchilla studies model/data allocation and treats the schedule as a training choice; the target argues the nonzero endpoint is itself suboptimal and can materially shift compute efficiency.

novelty_assessment: Reviewer inference after checking linear-schedule theory, WSD, schedule-free optimization, and AdamW EMA work: linear decay-to-zero was already theoretically and empirically motivated, and the EMA-of-updates view comes directly from Wang and Aitchison. The paper's substantive novelty is the controlled LLM-specific cross-sweep over peak rate, decay ratio, TPP, batch size, weight decay, and scale, together with the time-varying AdamW coefficient extension and unusually strong compute-equivalence result. The evidence supports adoption for similar known-budget AdamW runs, but frontier-scale savings remain unverified projections.
reviewer_notes: Read all 34 extracted pages, including downstream results, parameterization replications, weight-decay/batch grids, NanoGPT replication, scaling-law appendix, and the proposed horizon-free coefficient schedule. Competitor records were checked against primary arXiv pages on 2026-08-23.
